title: 50 Best AI Couple Photo Prompts
excerpt: A practical guide to creating realistic, cinematic and creative AI couple photos with stronger prompts, better composition and reliable identity preservation.
content: AI couple photography has become one of the easiest ways to turn two ordinary reference photos into cinematic concepts, travel memories, vintage portraits or romantic editorial scenes. The quality of the result, however, depends heavily on how clearly the image prompt describes the visual goal. A vague request such as “make a romantic couple photo” gives an image model too much freedom. A stronger prompt defines the relationship between the subjects, their pose, camera perspective, environment, lighting, wardrobe, mood and realism requirements.

The most important rule is to describe what should actually be visible. Instead of stacking adjectives such as beautiful, perfect, amazing and ultra-realistic, specify concrete visual information: where each person is standing, what they are doing, what the camera can see, how the light falls across the scene and what type of photography the result should resemble. Specific visual instructions are easier for an image model to interpret.

If you are using two reference photos, identity preservation should be treated as a separate requirement. Tell the model to preserve each person's recognizable facial structure, natural proportions, skin tone, hairstyle and defining features. Also make it clear that the two identities must not be blended into one face. This is especially useful for couple portraits where both people need to remain recognizable.

Composition matters just as much as facial accuracy. Decide whether you want a close-up, waist-up portrait, full-body photograph, mirror selfie or environmental shot. A close-up emphasizes expressions and faces, while a full-body composition gives the model more room to show clothing, location and body language. For Instagram, vertical 9:16 framing is often a practical choice when the final image is intended for a Reel or Story.

Lighting should support the story of the image. Warm sunset light can create a nostalgic romantic feeling, soft window light can make a café scene intimate, while directional street lighting can produce a cinematic night portrait. Describe the direction and quality of light rather than simply writing “good lighting.” You can also mention realistic shadows, natural highlights and believable reflections when the scene contains glass, mirrors, water or polished surfaces.

Wardrobe should be coordinated without making the couple look artificially identical. Instead of asking for matching outfits, describe complementary colors, fabrics and levels of formality. For example, one person can wear a neutral overshirt while the other wears a soft-toned dress. This creates visual harmony while preserving individual styling.

A useful workflow is to start with one of CreateLoom's detailed couple prompts, generate a first result, and then change only one major variable at a time. Change the location first, then lighting, then wardrobe or pose. If you change everything simultaneously, it becomes difficult to understand which instruction improved or damaged the result.

For romantic concepts, avoid forcing exaggerated expressions. Natural eye contact, a subtle smile, relaxed shoulders and believable hand placement generally create a more convincing photograph than overly dramatic poses. Include anatomy safeguards when necessary, especially for hands, fingers and overlapping arms.

For cinematic results, think like a photographer rather than a keyword collector. Mention lens perspective, depth of field, framing, foreground and background separation when they matter. A 50mm-style portrait perspective produces a different visual feeling from a wide environmental shot. Likewise, a shallow depth of field can isolate the couple, while deeper focus can emphasize the location.

When a prompt produces inconsistent results, simplify it. Remove instructions that compete with each other, keep the subject and composition clear, and put the most important constraints near the beginning. Strong prompts are not necessarily the longest prompts; they are the prompts where every major instruction has a purpose.

For Instagram content, couple prompts can also become repeatable Reel formats. You can show the two original photos, reveal the prompt, show the transformation and then direct viewers to the exact CreateLoom prompt page. This creates a useful journey from social content to a page where the visitor can copy and reuse the prompt.
### A simple couple-prompt structure

A reliable structure is: subjects → identity preservation → pose → clothing → environment → composition → camera perspective → lighting → mood → realism and anatomy safeguards → output requirements. You do not have to use every section every time. The structure simply prevents important visual information from being forgotten.
### Common mistakes to avoid

Avoid contradictory instructions such as asking for a close-up while also demanding a complete full-body composition. Avoid vague phrases that do not communicate a visible result. Do not overload the prompt with dozens of styles that fight each other. If the image model keeps changing a person's identity, strengthen the identity-preservation instruction instead of adding more aesthetic adjectives.
### Best workflow for consistent results

Choose the concept first, upload the appropriate reference images, use a detailed prompt, generate several variations, select the strongest composition, and then refine one variable at a time. Save the prompt version that produces the best result. Over time, this gives you a reusable prompt library rather than a collection of disconnected experiments.

CreateLoom's couple prompt collection is designed around this workflow. Start with a concept such as a mirror selfie, sunset portrait, rainy cinematic scene, café date or traditional couple portrait, then customize the details that make the image yours.

title: Best AI Selfie Prompts for Realistic Photos
excerpt: Learn how to write AI selfie prompts that preserve identity, create believable camera perspective and produce natural-looking lighting, poses and environments.
content: A convincing AI selfie is more than a portrait with a phone added to the frame. A real selfie has a specific camera distance, perspective, arm position, lens behavior, lighting pattern and relationship between the person and the environment. When these details are missing, an AI-generated selfie can look like a studio portrait pretending to be a selfie.

Start by defining the camera perspective. Decide whether the phone is held at arm's length, slightly above eye level, close to the face or positioned in front of a mirror. If the phone is visible, describe where it sits in relation to the face and body. If it is not visible, describe the perspective as a handheld front-camera photograph rather than a generic portrait.

Identity preservation becomes especially important when a reference photo is used. State that the person's recognizable facial structure, eyes, nose, lips, jawline, skin tone, hairstyle and natural facial proportions should remain consistent. Avoid asking the model to simultaneously preserve identity and heavily reshape the face through beauty filters or unrealistic facial changes.

Realism comes from small details. Mention natural skin texture rather than perfectly smooth skin, realistic hair strands rather than plastic-looking hair, believable fabric texture, natural shadows and subtle lens behavior. The goal is not to add every possible realism keyword; it is to tell the model what physical qualities should remain believable.

Lighting should match the location. Outdoor selfies can use soft daylight, overcast light or warm golden-hour illumination. Indoor selfies can use window light, bathroom lighting, bedroom lamps or café lighting. If the light source is behind the subject, describe the resulting rim light or exposure behavior rather than simply requesting “cinematic lighting.”

Backgrounds also need direction. A realistic selfie should have a believable environment that supports the story: a bedroom mirror, city street, café, airport, car interior, hotel room or beach. Avoid backgrounds that are so detailed that they compete with the subject. The face should remain the primary visual anchor unless the location itself is the concept.

Pose direction should be simple. A slight head tilt, relaxed shoulders, one hand holding a phone and a natural expression can be more convincing than a complicated pose. If the image contains hands, ask for anatomically correct hands and natural finger placement. This is particularly useful in mirror selfies and fashion shots.

For Instagram, vertical 9:16 composition is often useful. Keep important facial and outfit details inside a safe central area so that cropping, interface elements or Reel overlays do not cover them. If the image is intended as a profile photo or feed post instead, use the aspect ratio appropriate to that destination.
### A practical selfie-prompt formula

Use this sequence: subject and identity → selfie type → camera position → pose and expression → outfit → location → lighting → background → photographic characteristics → realism and anatomy safeguards. This keeps the prompt understandable and makes it easier to edit.
### Why some AI selfies look fake

Common problems include overly smooth skin, unnatural eye direction, distorted phone placement, incorrect reflections, inconsistent hands, unrealistic background perspective and facial features that drift away from the reference. These issues usually improve when the prompt explicitly defines the camera setup and identity requirements.
### How to refine a selfie prompt

Generate a first version and identify the single biggest problem. If the face is wrong, work on identity instructions. If the scene is wrong, simplify the environment. If the camera perspective is wrong, clarify the phone position and framing. Avoid changing every section at once because you lose the ability to diagnose what caused the improvement.
### Selfie ideas that work well for Reels

You can build repeatable content around mirror selfies, car selfies, airport selfies, rainy street selfies, café selfies, old-camera selfies and fashion selfies. A strong Reel can show the original reference, reveal the prompt and finish with the generated result. The exact prompt can then live on a CreateLoom page for viewers who want to recreate the concept.

title: Instagram Reel Ideas for AI Creators
excerpt: Build repeatable AI-content Reel formats around prompt reveals, transformations, comparisons, tutorials and themed series instead of relying on random ideas.
content: AI creators have an unusual advantage on Instagram: the content itself can demonstrate a transformation. Instead of simply showing a finished AI image, you can turn the process into the story of the Reel. The strongest formats make the viewer understand the result quickly and then give them a reason to stay for the reveal, prompt or comparison.

The first useful format is the prompt reveal. Open with the finished image or a compelling before-and-after, then show the prompt that created it. Keep the opening visually simple so the viewer immediately understands what changed. The exact prompt can then be linked to a dedicated CreateLoom page.

A second format is the before-and-after transformation. Start with the original reference photo, introduce the concept in one short line, and reveal the AI result. This works particularly well for couple photos, vintage transformations, cinematic portraits, anime versions and fashion concepts.

A third format is the prompt comparison. Create two versions of the same concept and change one major instruction, such as lighting, camera perspective, location or wardrobe. Then explain what changed. This turns a simple image generation into educational content and gives viewers a reason to comment on which version they prefer.

A fourth format is a themed series. Instead of making unrelated Reels, create a sequence such as “7 Couple AI Prompts,” “AI Selfie Ideas,” “Vintage Photo Week,” “Cinematic Portrait Series” or “AI Travel Photo Ideas.” Series create a recognizable content pattern and make it easier to plan future posts.

A fifth format is the tutorial Reel. Demonstrate a short workflow from reference image to final generation. Keep the tutorial focused on one outcome. A Reel becomes harder to follow when it tries to explain every setting, tool and prompt variation at the same time.

A sixth format is the challenge or experiment. Try to recreate a specific photography style, decade, movie-like atmosphere or editorial concept using an AI prompt. The value comes from the experiment and the result, not from claiming that every generation will be perfect.
### Hook ideas

The opening should communicate the visual payoff quickly. Examples include showing the final result before the process, presenting a surprising transformation, comparing two generations or asking a simple choice such as which version looks more realistic. Avoid hooks that promise something the Reel does not actually deliver.
### Turn one idea into several Reels

One strong prompt can become multiple pieces of content. The first Reel can show the result, the second can explain the prompt structure, the third can compare two lighting variations, and the fourth can show a different reference photo using the same concept. This is more sustainable than constantly searching for completely new topics.
### Use comments as content signals

Pay attention to the questions people repeatedly ask. If viewers ask for the prompt, create a prompt-focused Reel. If they ask which tool you used, make a workflow explanation. If they ask for another style, turn that request into the next concept. This lets your audience help shape the content calendar.
### Make the destination useful

If a Reel sends viewers to CreateLoom, the destination should immediately fulfill the promise made in the Reel. A visitor should be able to understand the prompt, copy it, share it and discover related prompts without hunting through the site. This creates a better experience than sending viewers to a generic homepage.
### A simple weekly system

A practical schedule could rotate between a transformation Reel, prompt reveal, comparison, tutorial, themed series entry and audience-requested concept. The exact posting frequency matters less than maintaining a repeatable format and reviewing what your audience actually responds to.

The goal is not to manufacture viral posts every day. The goal is to build a recognizable content system where every good idea can generate multiple useful pieces of content and where the best-performing concepts can be improved rather than abandoned.

title: How to Get More Views on Instagram Reels
excerpt: A practical framework for improving Reel packaging, retention, clarity and repeatability without relying on fake engagement or artificial view boosts.
content: Getting more Reel views is rarely about one secret setting. A Reel has to earn attention, communicate its idea quickly, give the viewer a reason to continue watching and make the content satisfying enough to share or revisit. For a new account, this can take experimentation because the system has little historical information about the audience that will respond best.

Start with the first frame. If the opening frame is confusing, viewers may swipe before understanding what the Reel is about. AI creators have an advantage here because the final generated image can often serve as the visual hook. Show the strongest result early, then explain how it was created.

The second priority is clarity. A viewer should understand the topic without needing to read a paragraph of tiny text. If your Reel is about a prompt, say that clearly. If it is a transformation, show the original and result. If it is a tutorial, make the outcome obvious before starting the steps.

Retention improves when the Reel has a clear progression. Think of the content as a sequence: hook → setup → transformation or explanation → payoff. Avoid long introductions before the interesting part. The viewer should feel that each second is moving toward something.

For AI-image content, several structures are naturally suited to this progression. You can show the finished image, reveal the reference photo, display the key prompt instruction, show the generation process and finish with the final result. Another option is a direct before-and-after where the transformation is the entire story.

Packaging matters too. Your cover, opening frame, on-screen wording and caption should describe the same concept. If the cover promises a couple-photo prompt but the first seconds show unrelated content, the viewer has to spend effort figuring out what they are watching.
### Do not confuse views with success

Views are only one signal. A Reel with fewer views but strong saves, shares, comments, profile visits or followers can be more valuable than a Reel with many passive views. Look for patterns across several posts instead of judging your strategy from one upload.
### What to check after posting

Review the retention pattern, shares, saves, comments, profile activity and follower response available in your Instagram insights. Ask practical questions: Did people leave immediately? Did the concept become clearer later than it should have? Did the result justify the opening? Did people ask for the prompt? These questions tell you what to change.
### Improve one variable at a time

If a Reel underperforms, do not change the topic, hook, editing, caption, music and format simultaneously. Test a stronger opening with the same concept, or keep the hook and change the presentation. This gives you a better chance of learning what actually affected performance.
### Avoid fake engagement

Buying views, likes or followers can make an account's numbers look larger without creating a genuine audience. It also makes performance data harder to interpret. If your goal is a creator brand, real viewers who care about your content are much more valuable than inflated numbers.
### Build repeatable formats

A repeatable format reduces creative fatigue. For example, you might create a recurring “Prompt of the Day,” weekly couple prompt series, AI transformation series or prompt comparison format. Once a format works, keep the underlying structure while changing the topic.
### Give viewers a reason to visit your profile

If the Reel demonstrates a useful prompt, the profile should make the next step obvious. CreateLoom can act as the detailed destination where viewers copy the exact prompt, explore related prompts and read supporting guides. The Reel earns attention while the website provides the deeper resource.

Growth is usually an iteration problem rather than a single-post problem. Publish useful concepts, measure what happens, identify the strongest patterns and improve the next version. Over time, this produces a much more reliable content strategy than chasing every viral trend.

title: How to Get Your First Brand Deal on Instagram
excerpt: A beginner-friendly framework for positioning your creator profile, building a simple media kit, finding relevant brands and sending professional collaboration pitches.
content: Getting a first brand deal is easier when your profile makes three things obvious: what you create, who your audience is and what a brand would gain by working with you. A huge follower count is not the only factor brands consider. A focused niche, credible content and an audience that matches the product can make a smaller creator interesting.

Start with positioning. If your profile is about AI image prompts, make that identity visible through your bio, recent posts and profile content. A brand should not have to scroll through unrelated posts to understand your niche. Consistency makes the account easier to evaluate.

Your content should demonstrate the kind of work a brand could buy. If you want software partnerships, publish tutorials or workflows. If you want fashion collaborations, create strong visual styling content. If you want creator-tool partnerships, demonstrate tools naturally in your content rather than waiting until you pitch.

Before contacting brands, prepare a simple media kit. It can include your niche, audience demographics when available, follower count, average or recent content performance, top-performing examples, content formats and contact information. Keep it readable. A brand representative should be able to understand the opportunity in under a minute.

Do not hide behind follower count. Explain your audience and the type of attention your content generates. For example, a creator whose audience repeatedly saves AI tutorials may be attractive to a creative software company because the audience has a practical reason to use the product.
### Find brands that actually fit

Start with products you genuinely understand and that naturally fit your content. Make a shortlist rather than sending the same message to hundreds of unrelated companies. Look at the brand's existing social content, target customer and typical collaboration style before pitching.
### Write a better pitch

A useful pitch is short, specific and easy to respond to. Introduce yourself, explain why the brand fits your content, propose one concrete content idea and provide the relevant profile or media-kit information. Avoid sending a generic paragraph that could have been addressed to any company.

For example, an AI creator could propose a Reel showing how a brand's creative tool turns a reference photo into several visual concepts, followed by a short tutorial or prompt workflow. The proposal becomes stronger because the brand can immediately visualize the deliverable.
### What to include in an offer

Possible deliverables include an Instagram Reel, Story sequence, carousel, tutorial, product integration, UGC-style video, website feature or bundled campaign. Be clear about what you are offering and what is included. If usage rights, exclusivity, whitelisting or paid amplification are requested, clarify those terms separately rather than assuming they are included.
### Pricing your first collaboration

There is no universal price that applies to every creator. Consider the deliverables, production effort, audience quality, expected usage, exclusivity and rights being requested. A simple content post and a campaign that gives a company permission to reuse your content commercially are not equivalent deals.
### Make your website part of the pitch

A creator-owned website can strengthen your professional positioning. CreateLoom can demonstrate that your content is connected to a larger creator ecosystem rather than existing only inside an Instagram profile. Your Brands and Contact pages should make it easy for a potential partner to understand the collaboration options and contact you.
### Follow up professionally

If a brand does not respond, one polite follow-up after a reasonable interval is better than repeatedly messaging them. Keep records of who you contacted, when you contacted them and what you proposed. Treat outreach as a pipeline rather than an emotional judgment of your content.

The first deal is often less about becoming famous and more about becoming easy to evaluate. Build a focused profile, publish evidence of your content quality, prepare a clear offer and contact brands whose products genuinely fit your audience.

title: How to Write Better AI Image Prompts
excerpt: Learn a repeatable framework for turning a rough visual idea into a clear AI image prompt with better control over subject, composition, lighting, identity and style.
content: A good AI image prompt is not simply a long list of descriptive words. It is a visual specification. The prompt should communicate what the model needs to know about the subject, action, environment, composition, camera perspective, lighting, style and important constraints. The objective is clarity, not maximum word count.

Begin with the primary subject. State who or what should appear in the image and what they are doing. If the subject is a person, include relevant characteristics such as approximate age group, clothing, pose and expression only when they matter to the visual result. Put the most important information early.

Next define the composition. Decide whether the image is a close-up, medium portrait, full-body photograph, wide environmental scene, mirror selfie or another framing. Composition determines how much of the environment appears and where the viewer's attention goes.

Camera direction can make a major difference. You can describe the viewpoint, focal-length style, camera height, depth of field or perspective when those characteristics matter. For example, a close portrait with shallow depth of field creates a different result from a wide environmental photograph where the background is intentionally visible.

Lighting should be described as a physical condition. Instead of writing only “beautiful lighting,” specify soft window light, warm sunset illumination, diffused overcast daylight, directional neon light, hard midday sun or another meaningful source. Include natural shadows and highlights when realism is important.

The environment should support the concept. If the subject is in a café, describe enough of the café to establish the scene without turning the prompt into a list of unrelated objects. If the concept is cinematic, the environment can include atmospheric details such as wet pavement, distant practical lights or subtle haze.

Style should come after the core visual information. Decide whether you want a realistic photograph, vintage film look, editorial fashion image, anime illustration, watercolor-like artwork or another direction. Mixing too many incompatible styles can reduce consistency.
### Identity preservation

When a reference photo is involved, identity should be explicit. State that the reference person's recognizable facial structure, natural proportions, skin tone, hairstyle and defining features should remain consistent. If two people are involved, make it clear that each identity must remain separate and recognizable.
### Negative or constraint instructions

Constraint instructions can help communicate what should not happen, particularly for anatomy, unwanted text, watermarks, duplicated objects or inconsistent facial features. Keep them relevant. A huge list of every possible failure mode can make a prompt harder to interpret.
### A reliable prompt structure

A useful structure is: subject → action or pose → identity requirements → clothing → environment → composition → camera perspective → lighting → mood → style → realism details → constraints. You can shorten or rearrange this depending on the image model and the complexity of the scene.
### Why more words do not always mean better results

Every instruction introduces another constraint. If the prompt contains conflicting directions, the model has to decide which one to prioritize. A concise prompt with clear hierarchy can outperform a much longer prompt filled with repeated adjectives.
### Iterate scientifically

Generate a baseline first. Then change one variable at a time. If the lighting is weak, change only the lighting. If the pose is unnatural, change only the pose. If the face drifts, strengthen identity instructions. Keeping variables controlled makes prompt refinement much easier.
### Use reference images carefully

Reference images can provide useful information about identity, clothing, pose or visual composition depending on the tool. Make the role of the reference clear in the prompt. If a reference is intended primarily for identity, say so. If it is intended for composition, specify that instead.
### Build reusable prompt templates

Once you find a structure that consistently works, turn it into a template with editable sections such as [SUBJECT], [OUTFIT], [LOCATION], [LIGHTING] and [MOOD]. This lets you create variations quickly without rewriting the entire prompt every time.

The best prompt-writing workflow is therefore simple: define the visual goal, describe the important physical details, preserve identity when needed, establish composition and lighting, generate a baseline, inspect the result and refine one variable at a time. CreateLoom's prompt library follows this practical approach so you can start from a structured prompt instead of a blank page.

title: Nano Banana AI Photo Prompts: The Complete Guide
excerpt: What Nano Banana actually is, why it became the tool behind most of this year's viral Instagram AI photos, and how to structure a prompt that gets a clean, identity-preserving result.
content: Nano Banana is the name that stuck for Google's image-generation and image-editing model inside Gemini, and by 2026 it has become the tool most people mean when they search for a “trending AI photo prompt.” Its popularity did not come from being the flashiest option on paper. It came from being unusually good at one specific thing people actually want: taking a real photo of a real face and changing the styling, outfit, setting or format around it while keeping that face recognizable.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. Most earlier image generators were built to create a scene from scratch out of a text description. Nano Banana behaves more like an editor you talk to in plain language. You give it a photo, describe the change you want, and it applies that change while treating the rest of the photo as something to preserve rather than something to reinvent. Once people realized this, the entire category of “turn my selfie into X” prompts took off.

This changes how you should think about writing a prompt for it. Instead of describing an entire scene as if nothing exists yet, describe the transformation. State what should change, state what should stay the same, and be explicit about the one thing most people forget: that the person's actual face is the anchor the whole image is built around, not a detail to be regenerated.

A dependable Nano Banana prompt usually has four parts. First, name the transformation directly — a 3D figurine, a traditional saree portrait, a retro film poster, a polaroid with someone else in frame. Second, describe the specific visual details of that transformation: textures, lighting, props, framing. Third, state the identity instruction on its own line so it does not get lost among styling details. Fourth, mention the output format if it matters, such as a square frame, a visible border, or a plain background.

The identity instruction deserves its own sentence rather than being folded into a longer description. Something like “preserve the subject's natural facial structure, skin tone and features exactly as shown in the reference photo” does more work than a dozen aesthetic adjectives. Nano Banana tends to respect an isolated, clearly stated constraint more reliably than one buried in the middle of a stylistic paragraph.

Most of the trend categories currently spreading on Instagram are really the same underlying skill applied to different concepts. The collectible-figurine trend asks Nano Banana to restyle a person as a toy while keeping their face. The traditional-saree trend asks it to change clothing and setting while keeping the face. The retro Bollywood-poster trend adds typography-style framing and film-grain texture on top of the same core instruction. Once you understand the pattern, you can adapt it to a concept nobody has tried yet.

The polaroid-style trends work slightly differently because they often combine two reference photos — a present-day photo and a childhood photo, or photos of two different people. Here it helps to name each subject's role explicitly (“the adult in the first reference,” “the person in the second reference”) so the model does not blend two identities into a single face, which is the most common failure in these prompts.
### A simple Nano Banana prompt formula

A workable structure is: name the transformation → describe the specific visual details → state the identity-preservation requirement on its own → specify format or framing if relevant. Keep each part to a sentence or two. Nano Banana responds better to a short, well-ordered prompt than to an exhaustive one.
### Common problems and how to fix them

If the face starts drifting from the reference, the identity sentence is usually too vague or too far from the front of the prompt — move it earlier and make it more specific. If the styling looks weak or half-applied, the transformation description is probably too short; add concrete visual details like texture, lighting direction and color rather than single adjectives. If two people's faces start blending in a multi-reference prompt, name each person's role explicitly instead of referring to “both people” as a group.
### Editing an existing generation instead of starting over

One underused feature of working with Nano Banana through Gemini is that you can keep the conversation going after the first result. Rather than rewriting the whole prompt because the lighting is slightly off, describe only the adjustment you want — “make the lighting warmer” or “move the light source to the left.” This mirrors how a real photo edit works and usually gets you to a usable result faster than regenerating from scratch each time.
### Building a repeatable workflow for Instagram content

Once a Nano Banana prompt produces a result you like, treat it as a template rather than a one-off. Swap the reference photo, keep the transformation instruction the same, and you have a repeatable format for a Reel series. This is exactly how most of the current viral trend formats spread — not because one image went viral, but because the underlying prompt structure was easy for anyone to reuse with their own photo.

CreateLoom's Nano Banana-compatible prompts are written with this structure in mind, so each one separates the transformation, the visual details and the identity instruction clearly — copy one, drop in your own reference photo, and adjust only the part that needs to change for your version of the concept.

title: Trending AI Photo Styles on Instagram Right Now
excerpt: A breakdown of the AI photo styles actually spreading on Instagram this year, why each one caught on, and how to adapt one into your own content instead of copying it exactly.
content: AI photo trends move differently from most Instagram trends. A dance or audio trend spreads because it's easy to copy with your body. An AI photo trend spreads because it's easy to copy with a prompt and a selfie — no skill, no editing software, no waiting. That's part of why the current wave of trends has moved faster and lasted longer than the filter trends that came before it.

The common thread across nearly every trend spreading right now is identity preservation. Earlier AI photo fads relied on stylized filters that changed your whole face into a cartoon or painting. The current generation of trends keeps your actual face recognizable while changing everything around it — which is a large part of why people are comfortable posting the results next to their normal photos.

The collectible-figurine trend is a good example. The prompt asks the model to reimagine the person as a 3D toy figure, complete with a display base and packaging-style presentation, while keeping the face a faithful likeness. It spread quickly because the novelty is instantly understandable in a single frame — you don't need context to “get” the image the way you would with a more abstract art style.

Traditional-outfit portraits, especially saree looks, are one of the most consistently searched styles on Indian Instagram this year. Part of the appeal is practical: not everyone owns festival-ready clothing or has time to get one professionally styled, and an AI version lets someone try the look before deciding whether to actually wear it for an event.

Retro Bollywood-poster styling is a slightly more theatrical trend, turning a normal photo into something resembling a 1990s film poster — spotlighting, grain, an ornate typography border. It works because it borrows a visual language most people in India already recognize instantly, so the joke or nostalgia lands without needing an explanation.

Polaroid-style prompts, including the versions that place someone next to a younger version of themselves or next to a person who isn't physically in the room, tap into something more emotional than the others. These tend to get shared privately — sent to a parent, a partner, or an old friend — rather than just posted publicly, which is part of why they keep resurfacing in different forms.

Cinematic portrait styles — moody studio lighting, neon-lit street scenes, film-grain edits — have stayed popular for longer than most single trends because they aren't tied to one specific gimmick. They function more like an aesthetic upgrade for an ordinary profile photo, which gives them a longer shelf life than a novelty format.
### How these trends are actually being searched

Search behavior around these styles clusters into a few consistent patterns: the tool name plus the style (“Nano Banana saree prompt”), the platform plus the intent (“Instagram trending AI photo prompt”), and increasingly specific variations of an established trend (“90s Bollywood heroine poster prompt” rather than just “Bollywood poster”). That last pattern is worth noting — once a trend is established, people search for more specific versions of it rather than the general idea.
### Why some versions of a trend look noticeably better than others

The difference between a convincing result and an obviously-AI one usually comes down to reference photo quality and how specific the prompt is about lighting and texture, not the concept itself. A blurry, badly-lit selfie will produce a mediocre figurine or saree portrait no matter how well-written the prompt is — the model can only work with what it's given.
### Turning a trend into your own content instead of a copy

The creators who get the most out of a trend adapt it rather than replicate it exactly. If a saree-portrait trend is spreading, a travel creator might apply it to a specific regional style tied to a place they're covering. If a polaroid trend is spreading, a comedy creator might apply it to an exaggerated, deliberately absurd pairing instead of a sentimental one. The format is the reusable part; the specific execution is where your own content stands out.

Because these trends move quickly, CreateLoom's trending prompt section is reviewed and updated as new patterns emerge, so the goal is to keep a current, honestly-labeled read on what's actually spreading — rather than treating any one style as permanent.

title: ChatGPT AI Photo Prompts for Instagram: A Practical Guide
excerpt: How ChatGPT's image generation actually behaves compared to other tools, where it's the stronger choice, and how to write and refine prompts for it specifically.
content: ChatGPT's image generation gets searched almost as often as Nano Banana's for a simple reason: a huge number of people already have ChatGPT open for something else and try the photo prompt there first, before ever looking for a separate tool. That habit alone makes it worth understanding on its own terms rather than treating every AI photo prompt as interchangeable across platforms.

The most useful thing to know about ChatGPT specifically is that it behaves conversationally. Rather than treating each prompt as an isolated instruction, it treats the conversation as an ongoing project you're refining together. That makes it well suited to a back-and-forth workflow: generate a first version, then describe exactly what to adjust in the next message instead of rewriting the whole prompt.

ChatGPT also tends to handle legible text inside an image more reliably than most alternatives, which matters for anything poster-like — a title, a birthday message, a name on a jersey. If your concept depends on readable text appearing correctly in the final image, that's a point in ChatGPT's favor over tools that are stronger at pure photorealism but weaker at typography.

For a first-message prompt, the same core structure that works elsewhere still applies: describe the subject and identity requirement, the transformation or scene, the composition, and the lighting or mood. What changes is how much you lean on the follow-up messages afterward. Where a single-shot tool needs everything specified up front, ChatGPT rewards leaving room to adjust after seeing the first result.

Identity preservation works a little differently here too. Rather than a single dense instruction, it can help to state it plainly and then reinforce it if a follow-up edit starts drifting — for example, if you ask for a background change and the face shifts slightly as a side effect, a short follow-up like “keep the face exactly as it was in the previous image, only change the background” is usually enough to correct it.

One common frustration people run into is over-stylization: asking for a specific aesthetic and getting a result that leans further into that style than intended, at the cost of realism. If that happens, it's more effective to explicitly ask for the realism to be dialed back in a follow-up (“make this look like a real photograph, reduce the illustrated or painted quality”) than to rewrite the entire original prompt.
### A ChatGPT-specific prompt formula

Open with subject, identity requirement and the core transformation in one message. Keep the first prompt moderately detailed rather than exhaustive — composition, lighting direction and mood are usually enough. Save fine-tuning (color grading, minor pose adjustments, background swaps) for short follow-up messages rather than trying to lock everything in on the first attempt.
### Getting good iterative edits

Be specific about what should change and explicitly say what should stay the same in the same message — “change only the lighting to golden hour, keep the pose and outfit exactly as they are” works better than “make it more golden hour.” Vague follow-ups tend to produce broader, less predictable changes than the original prompt.
### When to reach for ChatGPT versus another tool

ChatGPT is a strong choice when a project involves several rounds of back-and-forth refinement, when text needs to render correctly inside the image, or when you're already mid-conversation about the concept and don't want to switch tools. For a single, carefully pre-planned identity-preserving portrait where you already know exactly what you want in one shot, a tool built specifically around photo editing can sometimes get there in fewer attempts.
CreateLoom's prompt library flags which tools each prompt was written for so you can pick based on how you actually want to work — one detailed attempt, or a conversation you refine as you go.

title: How to Make AI Photos Look Real Instead of Fake
excerpt: The specific details that separate a convincing AI photo from an obviously artificial one, and the prompt language that actually fixes each problem.
content: There's a specific, recognizable look people mean when they say an AI photo looks “fake,” and it's rarely one big mistake. It's usually a handful of small physical inconsistencies stacked on top of each other — skin that's too smooth, eyes that don't quite focus on anything, lighting that doesn't match between the subject and the background. Fixing the biggest offenders individually does more than adding a general “make it realistic” instruction ever will.

Skin texture is the most common giveaway. Many models default toward smooth, evenly-lit skin because it's a safer average result. Asking explicitly for natural skin texture — visible pores, slight unevenness, natural texture rather than a retouched look — pushes the result away from that default and toward something that reads as a real photograph rather than a beauty filter.

Eyes are the second most common tell. Unnatural results often have eyes that are too symmetrical, too brightly lit compared to the rest of the face, or aimed in a direction that doesn't match the head's angle. Naming a specific gaze direction — looking slightly off-camera, or making direct eye contact with the lens — gives the model a concrete target instead of leaving it to guess.

Hands remain one of the harder problems for most image models, especially in poses where fingers overlap, hold an object, or rest against fabric. If hands are visible in your composition, an explicit anatomy instruction (“anatomically correct hands with natural finger placement”) measurably reduces the odds of an extra finger or an oddly bent joint, though it isn't a guarantee.

Lighting mismatch is a subtler problem that's easy to miss at first glance but registers instantly on closer inspection: a subject lit like they're indoors placed against a background that's clearly lit like outdoor daylight, or shadows falling in a direction that doesn't match the implied light source. Describing the light source once and its direction explicitly — rather than describing the subject's lighting and the background's lighting as if they're separate problems — keeps them consistent.

Reflections and shadows carry more weight than people expect. A mirror selfie with no visible phone reflection, or a person standing near a window with no corresponding shadow, breaks the illusion even when everything else in the frame is convincing. If your composition includes a mirror, glass, water or a polished surface, it's worth naming what that surface should realistically show.

Reference photo quality matters more than most people account for. A blurry, poorly lit or heavily-cropped reference photo gives the model less accurate information to preserve, and no amount of prompt refinement fully compensates for that. A clear, front-facing, evenly-lit photo is the single highest-leverage thing you can control before you even write the prompt.
### A realism checklist before you generate

Skin texture specified rather than left to default. Eye direction and expression named explicitly. Hands given an anatomy safeguard if visible. One consistent light source described for the whole scene, not the subject and background separately. Reflections or shadows addressed if the composition includes a mirror, window or glass surface. A clear, well-lit reference photo used as the starting point.
### When a prompt keeps producing an artificial result

Resist the urge to add more realism keywords on top of each other — stacking “ultra-realistic, photorealistic, 8k, hyperrealistic” rarely helps and can push a result toward an over-processed look instead. Identify which single element looks wrong — skin, eyes, lighting, hands — and address that one thing specifically before touching anything else.
### Realism isn't always the goal

Not every concept should aim for photographic realism. A cartoon sticker, an anime portrait or a poster-style illustration is meant to look stylized, and pushing those toward photorealism usually makes the result worse, not better. Decide which category your concept belongs to before applying any of this — these fixes are for photo-style prompts specifically, not illustrated ones.

Every prompt in CreateLoom's photo-style categories is written with these specific details already built in, which is part of why identity and realism tend to hold up better than in a prompt assembled from a generic adjective list.
